speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON RESUMPTION OP DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with leave of the house, and I hope leave will be granted, I should like to bring up the question of what date might be set aside for discussion of the question of capital punishment. There were two bills before the house, one introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough and the other by the hon. member for Vancouver East. After we had discussed the matter for a couple of days the question arose whether or not a further opportunity would be given to the house to discuss this very important measure, and also the problem in general of the infliction of capital punishment. On a number of occasions since questions have been asked as to when that date would be, I made it perfectly clear that we on this side of the house would be most anxious to have the fullest possible discussion of this question which is of such paramount importance.
My recollection is that the last occasion on which the matter was mentioned was July 18. There may have been later occasions but at the moment they do not come to mind. At that time the Leader of the Opposition asked this question, as found on page 6410 of Hansard:
Has the government any plans for the resumption of the discussion of capital punishment?
To which my reply was:
As the hon. gentleman knows, plans were made some weeks ago and were made known to the house. As soon as the legislative program and the estimates have achieved that degree of completion which I believe is necessary, then with the co-operation to which the hon. member for Laurier referred, I am sure that a day will be set aside for that purpose.
The Leader of the Opposition then added these words:
What degree of completion does the Prime Minister consider necessary so that we may resume the discussion?
To which I replied:
The order paper is a pretty good indication, together with the estimates still outstanding.
The hon. member for Assiniboia then added some comments in this regard but more particularly directed to the question of consideration of extending the vote to those 18 years old. I wish to give hon. members the opportunity to express themselves with regard to resumption of the debate on capital punishment. Any day that would suit hon. members would be acceptable to the government.
We have now arrived at that point where, if hon. members in various parts of the house desire to debate this subject, it will be done. To that end I ask not only for the views of the Leader of the Opposition but also for those of the two hon. members to whom I have already alluded, whom I feel sure the house would want to hear, as they have taken a particular interest in this matter and have respectively introduced bills in this regard.

Business of the House

I do not have to tell you, sir, or the house, of my 25 years' interest in this matter of the abolition of capital punishment. There was in the early days of the session a two-day debate, and the understanding was given by the Prime Minister that a third day would be made available. This matter is of such importance that I feel a third day of debate on a private member's bill, which I seconded, should not be held in the dying days of this session.
I believe, sir, that we had a very good discussion for two days. If my information is correct I believe that, at the conclusion of the second day of debate, there were in the neighbourhood of 37 members who still wanted to speak on this issue. I do not know quite how to put what I have in mind, but having debated the subject for two days and it now being near the end of this session, in view of my 28-year fight in parliament both in British Columbia and here against capital punishment, I would hate to see a hasty decision made in this house. It is not so much a matter of seeing whether the bill introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, which I seconded, would be defeated, but it is a matter which requires a quiescent, sensible and reasonable decision.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, much as it may break my heart, because I want to see my objective reached I am afraid, sir, it would not be reached if a decision were taken by the House of Commons to sit an extra day at this point in the session.
Therefore, because I believe in the objective and not in expediency, I hope the mover and seconder of this motion will agree with me that perhaps greater progress will be made toward our objective by agreeing now that a further day be not taken this session, because I believe from what I heard from the Prime Minister that consideration is being given by the government to the entire question of capital punishment and no objections have been raised to the matter being reinitiated at the next session of this House of Commons.
So, sir, on that basis I believe those of us who believe in the abolition of capital punishment might have our objective set back if at this time there were a further debate. Therefore, sir-and I am only speaking personally-I say I will accept the idea that there shall not be a further debate on capital punishment at this session. But it will be raised at the next session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister of South Africa has announced that a referendum will take place in that country, I think on October 5, to determine whether South Africa desires to become a republic. That decision is a matter for the people of South Africa, as was made abundantly clear in the communique following the prime ministers' conference in London. In the communique then issued it was made clear that the decision whether or not South Africa would then be admitted to the commonwealth would be a question to be decided at that time.
When I answered a question respecting this matter some weeks ago I made it clear that no undertaking had been given by Canada as to what Canada's attitude would be, for to do so might well constitute an interference with the rights of the people of South Africa or with the course that might be followed by the people of South Africa when voting on the referendum. I am glad that Prime Minister Verwoerd has underlined the correctness of that stand.
Further than that I would not want to go, for to do so might well constitute an invasion of the rights of the people of that country or might have an effect on the voting on the referendum, which is their own decision.

AH amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading-

-with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
The amendment before the house does not deal with any matter not already in the bill. What is the matter in the bill? The matter in the bill has to do with certain rights enumerated in subparagraphs (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) and (f) of clause 1. The matters referred to in the amendment are likewise the same kind of matters; they too refer to rights. The fact that the hon. gentlemen do not agree that these rights should be included does not change in any way the character of the rights or the matter involved in the amendment, unless one is prepared to argue that these are not rights. That cannot be the case, because every one of the rights enumerated in the amendment is a right that is contained in the declaration of human rights of the United Nations, a declaration which Canada supported, along with other countries of the world.
What hon. gentlemen have got to do, then, in order to succeed in their argument is to establish that the matter involved in the amendment is not the kind of matter involved in the bill. That is the issue, and it seems to me that the matter ought to be clearly settled, because of that obvious fact.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka argued on the merits. We are not arguing on the merits now. There are differences on the merits, of course. The hon. member argued whether or not these words should be included. This is not the point. That will be the question in debate, if Your Honour accepts the submission I make. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I have listened with much interest to the hon. member who moves this motion in his expression of his view that the rights enumerated in the proposed amendment are of the same order as those in the bill, because to my mind that is the crux of the decision I have to make.
I think it is clear that on third reading there is a fair scope for amendment, but by that time the principle of the bill has been approved by the house on second reading and therefore we cannot go beyond that principle. Furthermore, the bill has been before the committee of the whole house, where latitude is given to make changes which expand it or contract it within the principle approved on second reading.
Now we come to third reading and we have the bill in specific terms. I think it is obvious that third reading is intended as a final protection for parliament, to give the bill final consideration before it becomes law, and that there is a final opportunity to reject it or to refer it back to the committee if the house feels that the committee has not done what it should have done.
With that in mind my conception of a proper amendment on third reading is that it should not depart in kind; it should not introduce new principles. Quite frankly, as the hon. member read his amendment I could see that subparagraphs (c) (d) (e) (f) and (g) could be added to those principles in clause 1 of the bill which were declared as having existed and continuing to exist in Canada, and enumerated as the right of the individual to life, liberty etc., and the right of the individual to equality before the law, freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and freedom of the press. These are all matters which could be brought before the court where an individual could claim the right of protection. They do not involve the expenditure of money. They do not involve anything other than protection of those rights by the law of the land.
When I came particularly to the last two clauses of the amendment, however, it seemed to me that there one departs into a new and different area of legislation. I am not sure that it would not involve the expenditure of money if it means what it says, and it would therefore have to be preceded by a resolution. But in any event I do distinguish in my mind these rights in subparagraphs (i) and (j) of the amendment as being different in character and in order from those enumerated in clause 1, of the

Human Rights
bill, particularly a right such as the right of the individual to social security.
If that right means anything at all it means social security in the commonly accepted sense of the term. It means the right to maintenance by the state under certain circumstances, either because of ill health or unemployment or whatever it may be. Social security involves not the protection of a right which exists but the granting or the providing of something by the state as of right.
Subparagraph (i) goes on "and his entitlement to realize the economic, social and cultural activities indispensable for his dignity", etc. Clause (j) refers to "just and favourable remuneration ensuring for himself and his family an existence worthy of human dignity, and supplemented if necessary by other means of social protection." That surely involves the right to work at a fair wage.
If that sort of right is to be asserted in legislation, it is not something that arises simply by saying that it exists, and is therefore not of the order which can be protected by access to the courts. It involves, I think, not the protection of some personal right or right of property which an individual enjoys, but involves a right to have added something which he does not already have in the form of economic well-being.
I distinguish those two, and therefore feel that these clauses do go beyond the bill as it was originally drawn, as it was debated on second reading and as it appears now. Therefore I must, with great respect to the views expressed by the hon. member who proposed this amendment, find that it is not in order in its latter clauses and therefore not in order at all.

If debate is restricted to the matters contained in the bill, obviously amendments must be restricted to matters contained in the bill. I think that quotation from May puts the matter more clearly and more succinctly than it was put even in citation 418 in Beau-chesne, to which I referred.
I suggest that the ordinary meaning of those words is that you cannot deal with matters not contained in the bill. You will note that the word "matters" is plural, not singular. This I emphasize as seeming to me to indicate that May means there that where you have a bill with several clauses, the debate on third reading is restricted to what is contained in those clauses. If the debate on third reading is thus restricted so also must be amendments. So I come back to the point that since this amendment still contains matters which are

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has suggested that
1	might deal with this question.
The designations of naturalized Canadian citizen, Canadian citizen and British subject are all terms that are incorporated, and necessarily so, into the Canadian Citizenship Act. Section 26 of the Canadian Citizenship Act says that a Canadian citizen is a British subject. However, in Canada there are British subjects who are not Canadian citizens and that is, in accordance with their rights as provided for in the Canadian Citizenship Act.
Canadian citizens, then, are made up of three potential classes. There are those who were born in Canada and who become Canadian citizens by what is called jus soli, the law of the soil. Then there are British subjects, who may or may not become Canadian citizens, depending upon their wish. A naturalized Canadian citizen is one who has come from another country to live in Canada. That person may or may not wish to become a Canadian citizen. Let us say he comes from Czechoslovakia. He is allowed to stay here; he is not compelled to become a Canadian citizen, but if he becomes a Canadian citizen pursuant to the requirements of the Canadian Citizenship Act, then he is a naturalized Canadian citizen.

We find this statement in the amendment:
No naturalized Canadian citizen may be deprived of his citizenship and no naturalized British subject may be deprived of his status as a British subject under this act.
They who placed before parliament only a few years ago the legislation that makes this possible, now in the light of events which have brought about a transition of position have been impelled to endeavour to rectify the wrongs which they themselves committed. Turning again to the amendment we find these words:
No Canadian citizen may be deported from Canada under this act.
One does not want to go into the past, but the record of the previous administration with respect to the deportation of those whose only offence, as I said before, was confined to their colour is known to all. No matter how the hand of history writes, it cannot erase what was done. This amendment has that purpose, to lead the Canadian people to believe that those who did those things yesterday have changed and that the wrongs of yesterday are to be rectified today, although they took no measures to do that when they were in power following the war.
Turning again to the amendment we find these words:
No Canadian citizen or British subject may be detained under this act beyond a period of sixty days, unless the cause for his detention has been reviewed by an appropriate impartial tribunal which has reported to the minister or authorities authorizing the detention.
We asked for that on a number of occasions. We asked why it was that men were held against whom there was no evidence but only suspicion. We understood the incarceration of those people was in the interest of the maintenance of the security of the state, but we asked that some measures be taken to enable those persons deprived of the ordinary rights of Canadian citizens to have the opportunity of establishing their innocence. In effect, what was asked for in those days is now being sought by a devious course, instead of by direct amendment, to be introduced into a bill of rights for the preservation of Canadian life.
All these questions are deserving of consideration. All of them will receive consideration in the committee to be set up to cover the whole ambit and field of the War Measures Act. And then, in the light of all the circumstances, with a full realization of the necessity of maintaining undiminished the security of the state, the War Measures Act may be rewritten and those terms removed that are unnecessary and unjustifiable.

Surely the Prime Minister is not trying to impress us with the fact that a future parliament, which might have some hesitation about amending and taking out of this bill rights which have been put in it, would have less hesitation in taking out of the War Measures Act rights which are guaranteed and which are included in this legislation. This is a strange development indeed.
Here is the right hon. gentleman who throughout the decades, throughout his service in this parliament, has been most vehement and most persuasive in opposition to the War Measures Act; yet when he has the opportunity in this house to remove from that act some of the opportunity for the circumvention of human rights and fundamental freedoms, he denies this parliament the right to act. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if this legislation has any meaning at all; if the Prime Minister is sincere in trying to put into a bill of rights those human rights and fundamental freedoms which he hopes no future parliament will dare abridge; surely if he is sincere in this he will want to put in this bill today those further guarantees and protections so they cannot in any circumstances be circumvented in the future by the back door route or the devious route he himself has described. Surely, in the Prime Minister's own words, this bill of rights will have perhaps some effect; it will have a retarding effect on future parliaments. Perhaps it will. Indeed, they should be reluctant to remove from the legislation any of those human rights and fundamental freedoms which are guaranteed by this bill, inadequate as it is. Surely it is not sound to put these human rights and basic freedoms in the War Measures Act which can be changed by parliament at any time.
Now, if the Prime Minister wishes to follow a straight course, if he wishes to be logical and consistent in this matter, he should rise in his place and say that throughout the debate he has taken the position that human rights and fundamental freedoms should be included in this legislation which he himself has introduced so that future parliaments would be reluctant to remove them, and that he would not leave to any future parliament, even one under his own leadership, the possibility of debasing or removing any of the rights which might under any circumstances be put into the War Measures Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of general remarks that I intend to make at this time. I need hardly express to this house my feelings at this moment. You will appreciate what it means to me to be approaching, having regard to the attitude of members in all parts of this house, the legislative enactment of a framework of ideas of some of the deepest convictions that can come to human beings who believe in freedom.
I want to begin by a reference to the kind of Canada that is represented in this House of Commons, made up of many races. To a varying degree, the committee itself was the embodiment of those things that indicate to us the changes that have taken place in our nation in a period of 46 years.
I say 46 years because it was that number of years ago today that world difficulty that has continued since had its inception in the beginning of the first world war.
At that time freedom was accepted as representative of a concept generally held in the world, and in the intervening years we have seen those vast changes that have taken place. In large areas of the earth freedom

has been swept away. Indeed, since the beginning of the first world war we have lived in continuous conflict, either active or quiescent. In other words, since the first world war ended on the 11th November, 1918, with the exception of the actual days of hostility in the second world war there has been a continuous armistice. Today we are in that position. As we look back to 1945 we realize that in the intervening years more than one third of mankind has come under the domination of a philosophy materialistic and godless, to use the words of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) on an earlier occasion.
When one looks back 46 years and remembers the sentiments that touched us then, it would have been indeed unusual if anyone had then been able to look forward to the day when men of so many races would be joined together in the Canadian House of Commons in their devotion to the maintenance and preservation of those things that are dearer than life itself.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I remember those days. I remember the years from 1903 to 1914, when the west was being opened up. Hon. gentlemen in all parts of the house are in that position. People came from other lands, and it was asked whether the day would ever come when those from foreign countries would be able to become part and parcel of a great Canadianism. Yes, we were in that position, after the first world war; that while those who served were Canadians during the days of war and had "Canada" proudly on their shoulder pieces, at the end of the war they returned once more to their paternal racial origin, and all were proud of that racial origin. Those of us representative of that ever-increasing number of Canadians who were not of British or French origin hoped for the day when we would have a Canadian citizenship. I think of my early days in the House of Commons when I advocated that which through the years represented to me the embodiment of a great Canadianism. I wondered whether the day would come when we would build that Canada out of a polyglot of racial origins.
Well, look at the committee, sir. The committee represented the trustees of freedom, entrusted by the members of this house to bring about a Canadian bill of rights, was representative of the original races but representative as well of those of-may I go down the list as I see it-'Italian, German, Chinese, Norwegian, Ukrainian, Polish, German, Icelandic and all other races; yes, all of them Canadians in a House of Commons that never before had the type of

representation that we have today, representative of so many origins.
* This group of members, following the authority given them by the house, brought about many recommendations and ideas which, translated into legislative form, now form the bill which will shortly, I hope, be passed by this house. No Canadian can give sanction to bigotry. That is the essence, one of the major portions of this bill of rights. We exiled it in the days of war. We today, by legislative enactment, ensure that the hallmark of freedom is the recognition of the sacred personality of the human being that denies discrimination in any form.
As the moving finger of history has written in the last 50 years, I am more than ever convinced of the rightness of one view that I have held throughout my life; that the existence of discrimination anywhere in Canada is a denial of that citizenship which we Canadians espouse and have a right to express. I believe, too, that the existence of discrimination anywhere in the world is a potential seed-plot for war. As we strive for peace our consecration to the maintenance of human rights is a fundamental requisite.
What does this bill achieve? I do not intend to reiterate any of the details now well known to the house, but I do believe that the essence of the bill of rights may be summed up under a number of categories. First, within the legislative and constitutional competence of parliament, this is the first integrated statement of the principal rights in the fields of political activity and matters of conscience, and in the relations of the individual to the courts, to the law and to the state.
It is true that we state that these rights have existed in the past. They have. I shall not repeat anything that will be partisan at this time. All of us have some responsibility for the fact that these rights and freedoms have not always been maintained. Where interfered with, the individual has too often been denied his right of recourse to the courts. Surely there is a vast difference between having these rights existing in many areas of our public and private law, between a diffused and unco-ordinated expression of these rights spread throughout many cases and statutes, customs and conventions, and this effort to boldly state them in understandable form.
Second, this bill of rights is a statement of values; values expressed in terms of law, values expressed in substance and in procedure. This is a statement not only of rights in a narrow sense but of values. Third, the specific contribution made by this bill to the law should not be underestimated. It makes the assumption, as I said a moment ago, that
Human Rights
these rights have existed. It is true that the language of the bill with respect to discrimination, the power of the press, due process of law and the forceful succession of clauses setting out the freedoms referred to, means to me something more together than if each individual item stood alone. Clause 1 is a major summary of substantive law as it affects our fundamental freedoms and rights, and no court henceforth can be indifferent to the effect of this statement when faced with the task of interpretation of past or future statutes.
As I look at this bill of rights and the declaration of the existence of these rights in the past, I can see a tremendous task resting upon the courts when it comes to the interpretation of statutes already existing. I know there were many who felt that the social rights and social freedoms should be included. They are of high value, and they are our goal under Canadian law. But this bill of rights is intended to be a document which I hope will influence the behaviour of the courts in dealing with the traditional problems of the relations between the individual and the state. It is because of that fact, restricted as this bill is to those things which come within the federal jurisdiction, that many of the social freedoms and rights which may be or are within provincial jurisdiction ought not to be stated in a national bill of rights unless that bill of rights is effective not only nationally but provincially as well.
Furthermore, these are rights which require a type of individual action in the courts. The whole range of social security and welfare matters are questions of policy and decision which rest upon broad administrative action. I can see the day, if perchance we are as close to national agreement in this regard as some state the fact to be, when after having secured the right to amend our constitution in Canada our major action will be to have restated in Canada's parliament, with the agreement of all the provinces, the abiding principles of freedom as well as those freedoms which were described in the days of war as freedom from fear and freedom from want.
There are many who still hide behind the Maginot line of their own failure to endeavour to understand the bill of rights, and who have not yet appreciated the fact that it will be very difficult in days ahead for any statute today existing to be interpreted in a way which will do violence to the letter and spirit of these provisions. It will be very difficult for any statute to be drafted and enacted by parliament from this day on which will in any way deny the provisions of subparagraphs (a) to (g) inclusive

Human Rights
in paragraph 2. The day of arbitrary detention, the day when an individual did not have to be informed of the reason for his detention, the day when the individual was denied the right to obtain and instruct counsel, the day when a habeas corpus was swept aside by order in council is, I hope, a day of the past in so far as days of peace are concerned.
And even in wartime, subject to those restrictions which will ensure that even in days of danger we must not unjustifiably imperil the rights of the individual, we must not interfere with the rights of the individual in a spirit of administrative lawlessness or caprice on the part of those who have the administrative responsibility to keep order.
The day, too, of arbitrary behaviour by any tribunal, commission or board in dealing with persons before them by depriving a person of a fair hearing is past. Every free man is entitled not necessarily to attain what he hopes for but to have his day and to give his answer to those who would limit his rights.
I think the clause which was added yesterday regarding the right of the individual to an interpreter, while not as significant as some of the other general declarations, is further evidence of our desire in this parliament, representing the conscience of the Canadian people, to ensure that Canadians everywhere, whatever may be their maternal language, shall not be denied the right and the privilege of full answer.
There is placed on the Minister of Justice a responsibility charging him with his own duties in regard to all legislation and special duties with regard to this legislation, so that in the examination of those things which come before him for legislative enactment any denial of these freedoms shall immediately receive his attention. This is an important responsibility.
Doubtless in the days ahead the suggestion made by the hon. member for Fort William and other hon. members respecting a committee on human freedoms will receive the fullest and most sympathetic consideration of parliament. I believe, as I have said on many occasions, that we should have a committee similar in nature to the scrutiny committee in Great Britain, to the end that every step that would in any way derogate from the maintenance of our fundamental freedoms should be subject to the closest examination.
I would hope that some day uniformity may be achieved throughout this country, as I have said on more than one occasion, in those matters over which parliament does not have jurisdiction, either by some appropriate constitutional process arrived at

through consultation with the provinces or through the other means of the adoption by the provinces themselves of collateral provincial legislation to preserve the freedoms.
This bill recognizes the deep and sometimes, I fear, the deadly cleavage between the rights of peace and the duties of war. The amendment to the War Measures Act is something that will require to be considered, as well as the entire act, to the end that we shall bring about such changes as a committee may recommend that will have the effect of assuring that in days of war we shall not desert freedom in order to assure freedom.
I think there is a paradox in the position we sometimes take. We deny the freedoms in days of war. In the days of the last war freedom was the impelling motive that caused men to give their all. I sometimes wonder what the result would have been if it had not been for those who were our leaders then and who, whatever the fears and tribulations of the moment, were able to say as free men, "We shall not surrender". How different things would have been had they not taken that position. None of us would consider our lives when weighed against the awful consequences of the actions of those who would deny freedom.
This recognition that something must be done in order to assure a proper balance-[DOT] not a compromise but a proper balance-[DOT] between the needs of security and the maintenance of the wells of freedom in the hearts of a free people will be given in the setting up of this committee. This process of recognition commences in clause 6 of this bill. Provision is made in that clause that the powers-and the can be tyrannical-under the War Measures Act shall within 15 days after proclamation be brought before parliament. In doing so we put the responsibility for the continuance of the proclamation where it ought to be, namely in and on parliament.
I said at the beginning that it was difficult to express my feeliftgs at a time like this, and some will ridicule what I say as an emotional reaction. I have devoted-and I say it in all modesty-not an inconsiderable part of my life and interest to the problems of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Whatever the cynics may say they do not deny that feeling. Having been able to bring about a major change in respect of freedom in this country through the co-operation of hon. members in all parts of this house, gives to me a reaction of deep appreciation for the democratic process and for the fact that when the people realize that there is need of change, all the minds that are closed against change must ultimately give way.

I do not pretend that this bill by itself will create a free and responsible society. The plural elements that make up freedom we take for granted, but they are many and varied. The church, the press, the educational systems, the trade union movements, a free economy, a culture which is naturally disposed toward freedom and personal dignity; all these things make up the society which we call Canada where this kind of bill is possible and where it reflects them to a far greater degree than it can ever create them.
I think what we have done has been right. I think it has been for the good of Canada. I also think that our conviction that a belief in the guidance of God makes possible a realization that law, justice and morality can be combined in words and perpetuated in a statute and this has been shown in the experience of the days that have elapsed since the introduction of this bill on Dominion day to be justified.
All that is required now is for each of us, and for Canadians as a whole, to mobilize in their hearts the determination that we shall make freedom work to a greater extent than ever before. This bill as I see it, is a major step forward. It gives a warning, and I hope brings to a halt the relentless expansion of the wide powers of the state, exercised at the expense of the individual, which has been a characteristic of all freedom-loving countries in the past 46 years. This outgrowth of the days of war, during which we made shortcuts through democratics rights under the excuse of need and contributing to efficiency, must be brought to an end.
I think that this bill will do its part to halt the march which has become ever more general since the outbreak of the first great war. The concept of efficiency has in the experience of 46 years brought about changes in democratic thinking that too often denied the rights of the individual. This bill will do its part to prevent unnecessary and unjustifiable interference with the rights of the individual by the state. To the average Canadian it will constitute a solemn declaration that we the Canadian people have the right to have our rights preserved. We have the right not to have determined what is right for us by others who are placed above the courts. It will determine now and for the future, in other words, that the dignity of the human person shall be maintained in equality under law and always without discrimination.
The purpose of the bill will be to achieve order and more liberty under law. This bill of rights will, I hope, establish a principle for all Canada which political passions will
Human Rights
not dare to destroy. It will set up an altar of freedom that will ensure that the minority will not be unjustly treated by the majority. This is of the essence of freedom. It will place before Canadians a declaration in favour of a government of laws, not men. It will make individual Canadians strong in the knowledge that under law the state shall not interfere unjustly with the person.
The principles of freedom are never final. Freedom is not static. It cannot be fixed for all time. It either grows or it dies. It grows when the people of a country have it in their hearts and demand that it shall be preserved. I would be the last to contend that any document made by man, however impressive, can assure freedom; but I think that what we have done will provide an anchor for Canadian rights. The ultimate assurance of them must always be a vigilant people, vigilant to invasions of and intrusions on their freedom; for, sir, when the spirit of freedom dies in the hearts of men no statute can preserve it.
I am glad of this day. To all members in all parts of the house I say I hope that in the years ahead these days will be looked back upon and that those who follow us will say that whatever the disagreements in detail, there was a united parliament and that in that parliament, they builded better than they knew.

Mr. Speaker, in the serene calm of post debate and the calm which the Prime Minister's rather complete summation of a splendid piece of legislation, I should like to make one or two personal observations. Certainly, it is thrilling for me to realize that I live in a free country, in which there is a free parliament, and in which such a piece of legislation can be enacted. I came to Canada, as my colleagues in the house know, rather a young boy with my parents. It was through the freedoms which we were able to enjoy in this country, those which existed on our arrival and those which continued to be improved and enlarged upon, that it was possible for me to become a citizen of this country and a member of this free parliament. It was in virtue of the citizenship act, which was enacted by a wise government, and in virtue of all the rights and freedoms which subsequent parliaments and legislation gave, that not only I, but all new Canadians joyfully welcome this bill of rights, not only in its entirety but also the spirit and the means by which it was enacted.
When the bill was introduced, some of us thought that it could be improved upon. As the Prime Minister so eloquently described,

Human Rights
the composition of the committee was arranged in such a way that all shades of opinions could be brought forward. I feel that as a result of the services which the committee so devotedly performed, and I think the Prime Minister agreed with this and I think he has said it, a better bill came out of the committee than went into it.
Some of us thought that perhaps it should have been more complete. I was interested to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) say during the course of the discussion that as time passes and as necessities arise, more freedoms and more rights, if they can be found, will be created. Some of us thought that not all were included that might have been, but if some were not included, I feel this was done with the best of intentions and the best of good will on all sides. One cannot always say with certainty that one is right. I had the thought, for example, that the right to Canadian citizenship is one of our basic human rights and I expressed some views on that during the course of the debate. I may not be right; I may be wrong. Perhaps those who advanced arguments against its incorporation in the bill were right, but it is quite possible that time will show that it is one of those human rights which Canadians should be privileged to have.
When I heard the Prime Minister invoke the Almighty I was touched, I was moved. I am rather pleased, yes, proud, that we have invoked the sacred name of God in the preamble, because to me it is a sanctification of the whole measure, and personally I am grateful to my leader who first suggested that a preamble should be incorporated in the bill. I also know that in the special committee the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and other members pressed for the inclusion of a preamble. When one reads even the first paragraph of the preamble he cannot help but be moved by the aura of sanctity which now surrounds this magnificent piece of legislation. Let me read the first paragraph of the preamble.
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions;
In invoking the sacred name of God, Mr. Speaker, we all acknowledge that He is the one and the same God from whom we all seek divine guidance and wisdom in our duties and responsibilities as servants of the people of a great country. It is God who is the fount of justice, righteousness, compassion and charity; it is God to whom we turn for solace and comfort in adversity and it is

God who guides the destinies of all of us, regardless of the place, means or language by which we beseech Him.

Mr. Chairman, when I started to make my opening remarks yesterday I was referring to the three cardinal principles


which govern our defence policy, namely that of the deterrent, that of collective security and that of forces in readiness.
The first of these, the deterrent, is brought about by the consequences of a war involving the use of nuclear weapons which are so terrible that we must make every effort to prevent such an occurrence. Whether our commitment is to NATO, to the defence of this continent or to the United Nations, we have undertaken such commitments in every case on the basic assumption that they will all contribute to the deterrent to aggression.
The second principle which I referred to was the requirement for collective security. The complexity of modern warfare coupled with the high cost of new weapons has made it impossible for any one nation to maintain adequate unilateral defences. This knowledge has resulted in Canada joining with other like-minded nations in such collective defensive alliances as NATO and NORAD and with others who are contributing to peace preserving forces of the United Nations.
Since events in the Congo are of topical interest at the moment I outlined briefly how we were assisting the United Nations force which is being assembled in the Congo to restore order and to prevent the outspreading of destruction which might possibly lead to war.
The final point I made was that if a deterrent was to be successful, if the collective forces of the west were to be effective, forces in being are required. There will be no time for a general mobilization as we have known it in the past, such as that which followed the outbreak of the first world wax; and it is significant that today, August 4, is the anniversary of that first global war. There would be no time to regroup or reinforce the forces in the field. We must have regular forces well trained and well equipped to ensure that the deterrent philosphy will prevail.
When the committee rose last night I was discussing Canada's contribution to these deterrent forces of the west, and I was pointing out that no part of the NATO area has been absorbed by the soviet since 1949 and that this was not solely due to the threat of massive retaliation. The fact that substantial land forces with adequate technical support have been maintained in Europe has been responsible for the continued peace of that area.
Canada's contribution of one brigade group and the Canadian air division has not been large, but the fact that we are there in position well equipped and highly trained has had a psychological and moral effect on the alliance as a whole as adding to the over-all

effectiveness of the forces available. Certainly the retaliatory forces of the stragetic air command of the United States are a major part of the deterrent, but if that portion of the deterrent is to be successful it must have the capability of being able to reach stragetic targets in the Soviet union.
To facilitate that we have established four refuelling bases in Canada. From these refuelling bases tankers can supply, if necessary in the air, the bombers as they pass over, and hence extend their range.
An adequate warning must also be given to prevent the SAC bombers from being caught on the ground and sufficient protection must be available to safeguard their bases. In this regard Canada plays an important part. Canadian land space is essential in the maintenance of the required warning system. The radar lines which have been mentioned are effective against the manned bomber.
Here again it has been suggested that since an attack on this continent will now be by missile there is no further use for the radar lines. The fact is that at the present time and in the immediate future any attack on this continent would consist of a combination of both missiles and manned bombers. The Russians have a large number of manned bombers still in service in their air forces. To give up all defences against manned aircraft at the present time would be inviting disaster.
Production of the intercontinental ballistic missile by the Soviet union is not estimated to be in sufficient quantity at the present time to ensure a successful attack-that is successful from their point of view-against the military and industrial targets of this country.
Certainly if there were no defences against the manned bomber Russia has enough aircraft which, equipped with nuclear bombs, could create sufficient devastation to justify the opinion that an attack would be successful. The radar lines, interceptor aircraft and surface-to-air missiles are therefore necessary as long as there is a threat of a manned bomber attack and since Canadian territory and Canadian airspace are inexorably involved in the successful defence against such an attack, it is to Canada's advantage to continue to be a partner with the United States in the joint air defence command known as NORAD.
It has been made perfectly clear that at the present time there is no defence against the ICBM. An early warning system known as BNEWS, the ballistic missile early warning system, is being established to detect the actual firing of such missiles. Canada has made a substantial contribution toward this
79951-0-477
Supply-National Defence warning system by providing the communications between the warning centres and the centres of population. Extensive research work in which Canada participates is proceeding to devise a method to combat these ICBM's.
I should like to refer at this time to statements that I made in the committee concerning the activities of our research program. I said:
In the event of an attack most ICBM's are likely to arrive in North America from a northerly direction. A special problem exists here because of the presence of the aurora borealis which tends to play havoc with radio devices. Radar beams can be seriously disturbed when the aurora is prevalent. Defence research board had for some time been investigating radio communications in the north and was well equipped to undertake a research program involving the aurora. In recognition of this fact, the United States offered to cooperate and loan to Canada a very powerful radar now installed at the Prince Albert radar laboratory. The scientific program of this laboratory is agreed with the United States authorities but full operational control is in Canadian hands. Much useful data already has been obtained. Defence research board scientists have also worked out measuring techniques for radio reflections from various types of warhead.
Another defence research board program is designed to differentiate between a warhead and the other parts of an ICBM rocket wihch would be in space when such missiles have been fired. In particular, I might mention a program at the Canadian armament research and development establishment where projectiles are shot at high speed down indoor ranges in tubes in which a vacuum has been produced, thus simulating the conditions in the upper atmosphere. This program has been of great interest to our United States partners, and a number of agencies concerned with anti-ICBM problems have been awaiting the results of CARDE tests in order to use them in their own program.
Further along I said:
The D.R.B. and the R.C.A.F. now are actively engaged in a co-operative United States-Canada program with instrumented aircraft in the south Atlantic connected with missile firings from Cape Canaveral. These tests are designed to determine what an incoming ICBM looks like.
When an incoming ICBM has been detected and identified, a missile must be launched from the ground to intercept and destroy it. Time is of the essence and such a missile must be fired at a few moments' notice. Many missiles are now using liquid propellants which require considerable time for preparation before firing. A solid propellant capable of instant readiness is obviously the requirement of the future. D.R.B. scientists have been working for some time in the propellant held and, in particular, have been concerned with low temperature characteristics of such propellants. It is believed that these characteristics will be most important in an anti-missile missile. The work conducted looks very promising.
I could give many other examples of where Canadian scientists are spending their endeavours in defence research and are co-operating to a very successful extent with their United States colleagues.
In this year's estimates funds are provided for two items of equipment which on account of their capability have caused some

Supply-National Defence comment. I refer to the Bomarc surface-to-air missile which is to be installed at sites near North Bay and La Macaza and the CF-104 aircraft which is to replace the F-86 Sabres of the eight squadrons in the R.C.A.F. air division in Europe.
The subject of the Bomarc consumed a considerable amount of time in this session of parliament. Due to the fact that it is a weapon being developed in the United States the comments that have been made here have been based on reports emanating from that country. Press and unofficial reports have been varied to say the least. The fact remains that after a number of trials in the testing of this weapon and discussions in the debates preceding the authorization of necessary United States funds for its continued development and procurement, the Bomarc has been accepted and now is considered an effective weapon capable of adding materially to the over-all deterrent and anti-aircraft defences of both Canada and the United States.
The units which are being established here and in the United States will provide coverage from Winnipeg to the Atlantic coast and are sufficiently dispersed and have sites so small in area as to obviate the likelihood of destruction from an intercontinental ballistic missile. From the trials that have been recently undertaken, the Bomarc with a designated range of over 400 nautical miles and with an effective guidance system, will add significantly to our defences.
Construction work is proceeding at the two Bomarc sites, the one at North Bay and the one at La Macaza. The cost of these two sites to Canada will be approximately $12 million. Construction will continue throughout the winter and will be completed by the time the Bomarc launchers are available.
I think the real point of contention with regard to both the Bomarc and the CF-104 is that both these weapons systems have the capability of being armed with a nuclear warhead. While there are no funds allocated in this year's estimates, it has also been announced that the Canadian army is to procure the Honest John launcher and associated surface-to-surface missile, the 762 mm. rocket. This weapon, too, has a nuclear capability.
The Prime Minister has on a number of occasions made Canada's position clear with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons. Speaking in the House of Commons on July 4, 1960, as reported at page 5653 of Hansard of that date, and referring to remarks he had made on an earlier occasion, the Prime Minister said:
On February 20, 1959, as reported on page 1221 of Hansard, I set forth the views of the Canadian government with respect to this matter, and they remain unchanged. At that time I set forth, as I
[Mr. Pearkes.l

say, that the full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads, and that of course was referring to Bomarc and other defensive weapons.
Later on he said:
In these circumstances negotiations are proceeding with the United States in order that the necessary weapons can be made available for Canadian defence units if and when they are required.
I think it will thus be agreed that the weapon systems that are being procured require nuclear warheads to reach their full effectiveness. To refuse or to neglect to have these available when required would place an intolerable handicap on our defences. The defensive weapon can only be used when hostile bombers are in Canadian air space; but these Bomarc weapons and the interceptors which may be flying through Canadian air space are defensive weapons only to be used, and their nuclear warheads only to be used, when attack is imminent and hostile bombers are actually in Canadian air space over Canadian territory.
To declare in advance that we would never use such weapons would weaken immeasurably their deterrent effect. Do not let us overlook the importance of the deterrent. I emphasized that many times during the course of this speech. Thus, if we announce that we are not going to use them we would be decreasing our ability to prevent war, which is the main object of all our defence preparations. Such a declaration would give a would-be aggressor great comfort and would facilitate the preparations of his plans, as he would know the limitations of our defence.
When discussing this matter on July 2, 1959 the Leader of the Opposition made this point when referring to the use of nuclear weapons, as reported at page 5371 of Hansard:
Tactical nuclear weapons have now been reduced to a point where they can be used by small formations against purely military targets. They are conventional almost in the sense that they are ordinary weapons with nuclear ammunition, but used in almost the same way as if it were ordinary ammunition. Second, if these weapsons were not used, NATO forces in Europe would be facing armies which had them and would not hesitate to use them. Unless we can get international agreement on this matter, the resulting military disparity created might well be considered intolerable to NATO morale. If the Canadian forces were deprived of these weapons or were not permitted to use them-this is a consideration which no doubt the government has very much in mind-their morale could hardly be expected to remain very high if they were serving alongside NATO forces which had these tactical nuclear weapons.
This records very definitely the opinion of the Leader of the Opposition, speaking for the Liberal party, as to his views on the use of nuclear weapons.
The Bomarc, the CF-104, the Honest John, will not be coming into service with the

Canadian forces until late in 1961. What we are undertaking and what has already been made perfectly clear is that we are discussing with the United States arrangements which will be acceptable to both countries as to conditions under which such weapons would be available to Canada if and when required. We are cognizant of the United States law on this matter. We are also firm in the conviction that the use of those weapons by Canadian forces should be at the discretion of the Canadian government. We are, therefore, going ahead with the procurement of the vehicles which can use these nuclear weapons, but the decision as to the acquisition of the nuclear warheads depends on circumstances which might develop sometime in the future.
In the past year great progress has been made in another aspect of our defence policy. I am referring to the part the Department of National Defence plays in survival operations. Our defence philosophy is, as I have said before, based on the deterrent but the possibility of the deterrent failing to prevent an outbreak of war calls for steps to be taken to ensure the survival of our country under these distressing circumstances. It is admittedly an awful eventuality, but the fact that we are taking such precautions is, in effect, an added insurance for survival.
As hon. members know, last September an order in council was passed assigning to various government departments, including the Prime Minister's office, various duties relating to survival. The Canadian army has been designated as the co-ordinating body within the department to carry out such duties as were set out in that order. Excellent progress has been made in the training of both the regular and the militia forces in survival operations. A great deal of equipment has already been obtained and the procurement of additional rescue and survival equipment is included in this year's estimates. Communications have been broadened and emergency regional headquarters are being constructed. I dealt with this in some detail when speaking before the estimates committee, and I should like to refer to some of the statements that I made there, as they define clearly the responsibilities of and the progress which has been made by the defence department in this respect. When dealing with national survival I said:
It is essential for the preservation of Canada as a nation that there should be continuity of civilian government in order to provide guidance and leadership, especially in the event of a nuclear attack. Each provincial government must be closely connected with the central federal facilities for emergency government through a highly efficient communications system.

The responsibility for establishing the system rests with the Canadian army. Progress has been made in this respect. I continue:
Regional centres are being established in each of the provinces. There will be some variation in their size and character, depending on a number of factors including the size of the population to be served, the likelihood of the provincial capital coming under direct attack, and particularly the emergency communications system and its technical requirements. The centres will be limited in size but will be sufficient to ensure the required operational capability.
Then I went on to describe in detail the responsibilities which the Department of National Defence had assumed in this respect.
Provision of technical facilities and the operation of a system to give warning to the public of the likelihood and imminence of an attack.
That communication and warning system has now been established. It is manned down to the provincial regional centres on a 24-hour a day basis and is being extended to every large municipality and centre throughout the country.
Determining the location of a nuclear explosion and the patterns of fall-out, and giving the necessary warning of fall-out to the public.
Once a warning of an impending attack has been given, should nuclear bombs fall on any part of Canada it is necessary to advise the population as to where the fallout is likely to come down on various areas. The pattern of the fall-out is not the same from one day to another and it is necessary to set up a grid across the country. Such a grid is being set up with some 2,000 or more detecting centres being established. These are known as radiation reporting centres and they are in communication with the provincial centres.
I do not intend to repeat all I said on national survival during the committee's meetings. It is all included in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee and in the pamphlet which I issued at the conclusion of those hearings. I do not want to repeat what I said at that time other than to say that the regular forces in Canada and the members of the Canadian militia are assuming these duties in a capable manner and with further training will provide a nucleus of men experienced in many ways with the various facets in which they will be involved in ensuring survival in the face of a nuclear attack.
I should like to say a special word about the militia and the other reserve formations, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve and the auxiliary squadrons of the R.C.A.F. Changes in the nature of the threat, new weapons and so on have dictated a change in the role of
7558	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence these bodies. As a result some have said that the need for these forces is reduced. That is not my view. The magnitude of the problem which would face this country in the event of a nuclear attack would require the largest possible body of trained and disciplined personnel. Those who give of their time and energy to ensure that we will be ready for whatever comes deserve the gratitude of all Canadians.
We are making good progress in supplying the militia with survival equipment. This summer many militia men attended training camps in which survival exercises were carried out in all commands across the country. From the reports I have received they have shown commendable enthusiasm and have made remarkable progress with their training.
To sum up, Mr. Chairman, I trust that what I have said with regard to our defence policy and the commitments we have undertaken to implement that policy have made clear our present position. We do have a very definite defence policy aimed, as it always should be, at preserving the security of our country, and the fact that our country continues to be secure indicates the success of that policy.
Critics outside this house can propound at length as to what is wrong with defence but unburdened by responsibilities their criticism is generally destructive, rarely constructive. In their lack of responsibility they have an advantage over the government. As Minister of National Defence, with the responsibilities that devolve on my position, I am required to make constructive decisions which will maintain the efficiency of our forces. I think that the steps we have taken in recent times with regard to the organization of our forces and in respect of new equipment either issued or on order have and will materially improve the contribution we are making to the overall deterrent and the peace preserving forces in many parts of the world. Our forces are well trained and of high calibre and wherever they serve they are making a vital and effective contribution to our collective defence efforts. We have every reason to be proud of their endeavours in this field.
Before I sit down, I should like to make reference to the reported speech of the hon. member for Trinity.

The report indicates that it was delivered in the house. The report reads in part as follows:
The Liberals, after three years of agonizing indecision, finally came out today with their own defence policy-one that would involve several breaks with present policies of Canada and the United States.

Paul Hellyer, Liberal defence critic, placed the new Liberal defence platform before the commons in a major policy speech.
Then the article goes on to indicate what he advocates. If I believed the article was true I would offer my apologies for the hon. member for not being here when he delivered that speech. However, I wish to extend my sympathy to him because he has been the victim of an irresponsible and unscrupulous newspaper reporter who, in order to obtain a newspaper scoop, did not hesitate to publish in advance an article based on the copy of the speech which I presume the hon. member handed to him.
I should like to say a few words about the main points made in that speech. As found in the article, the first one is:
No nuclear weapons for use on Canadian soil or in Canadian air space.
I dealt with that a few minutes ago and if that is the Liberal policy, if they are prepared to sacrifice the efficiency of our deterrent and the means of destroying hostile aircraft when they are over Canadian cities and armed with nuclear weapons; if they wish to say that Canadian forces are not to have nuclear weapons for the very purpose of defending Canadians, I hope they will go throughout the whole country declaring that policy. It is quite obvious that that policy is diametrically opposed to the policy announced by the Leader of the Opposition which I referred to in the debate a few minutes ago. The next point is:
Scrap plans to build the CF-104 supersonic jet interceptor for the R.C.A.F. air division in Europe, a project now under way at a cost of $400 million.
As I explained last night, the supreme allied commander in Europe asked us if we would re-arm and re-equip the squadrons of the air division which are now armed with the F-86 Sabre. After exhaustive inquiry into many different kinds of aircraft we decided that the F-104 was the most suitable aircraft which could be chosen for the role which the supreme allied commander had asked our squadrons to carry out. Having made the decision that the F-104 was the most suitable, we were happy to find out that other NATO countries who had made similar investigations to what we had had also decided the F-104 weapon would be the most suitable to them.
I mentioned yesterday that Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Italy were all procuring this same type of weapon. This means that many of the NATO forces have a uniform type of aircraft. It may be of interest to know that the minister of national defence of the Netherlands had this to say

when he announced the selection of the F-104G for the Royal Netherlands air force:
The Netherlands government has decided to buy the F-104G to replace jet fighters now in use tor the air defence and tactical air forces. Prior to taking this decision both the Netherlands and Belgium air forces made a comparative study of the problems involved. Both air forces wanted a type which was capable of both offensive and defensive tasks in order to give a small air force the most efficient operational effect. The Netherlands sees in the F-104G, the best plane to meet the double role requirement. Since the German and Canadian governments have already purchased the same type of aircraft, the "Star Fighter" also offers the additional advantage of a high degree of standardization.
This explains why we cannot subscribe to the points suggested in this speech, one of which reads:
Scrap plans to build the CF-104 supersonic jet interceptor for the R.C.A.F. air division in Europe, a project now under way at a cost of $400 million.
Acquire from the United States a supersonic jet interceptor to replace the CF-100 in Canadian home defence squadrons.
I explained yesterday that this latter matter was being given the most careful consideration by the government. I explained the difficulties that there were in reaching a quick decision, and I informed this committee that we would very soon be able to make a definite decision.
The next recommendation in the report of this speech is:
Scrap the seven new destroyer-escorts now being built for the Royal Canadian Navy at a cost of $26 million apiece, and replace them by ships designed to act as combat troop carriers and supply vessels.
I do not know how combat troop carriers are going to protect the shores of this land against submarines. I should think that combat troop carriers might themselves be very vulnerable to attack by submarines. Then the article continues:
Scrap the Bomarc-SAGE program for anti-bomber defence of the North American continent.
We find here what is described as the bold proposals, representing the Liberal policy, and they turn out to be nothing but scrap, scrap; scrap the CF-104, scrap the seven destroyers, scrap the Bomarc-SAGE, scrap nuclear weapons. It is a policy of scrap, and there is nothing constructive about it at all. If those are the bold proposals which the hon. member has been hoping to have an opportunity of propounding this afternoon and which he was so anxious to get before the Canadian public that he issued this to the press gallery so that it might be out on the wires across the country, I suggest to him that now is the time to scrap that speech.
Oh, oh.

speechtext:
