the minister of defence.

Notwithstanding that, we
think it is worth while to put forward proposals and to enter into the type of discussion and debate which will assist, not only the gentlemen of this house but the people in the country at large to understand the many complex and difficult problems involved in this whole matter of national defence at the present time. It is a pleasure, in this sense, to give to the committee this statement. My leader will be speaking later in the debate and he will augment and amplify some of the ideas that will be put forward at this present time.
First, Mr. Chairman, Canada's defence policy, as has been stated by the minister, is -or at least should be-an instrument of our foreign policy. Our national objectives are to preserve the peace while at the same time guaranteeing those fundamental freedoms which we hold sacred, and these objectives are only possible, as the minister has again stated today, through collective arrangements.
This position is fundamental and, I am glad to say, bipartisan, because obviously a small country of the size of Canada is not in a position to defend itself against any possible aggressor. Peace is our only sure defence today, and the great objective of defence, as well as of foreign policy, must be to preserve it. If it is lost, and a general war breaks out-which, as the minister has said, would mean nuclear war-then there

is no defence that would ensure protection against universal destruction, and there is no defence of any kind through national effort alone. There is no sure defence and there is no possible victory. We can, however, as part of the defence coalition, dedicated to peace and freedom band together to prevent war by making it disastrous for any aggressor to break the peace.
The minister has repeatedly referred to deterrent as the solution in trying to avoid war, by making it disastrous for any potential aggressor to break the peace. Canada as a part of such a coalition can best achieve that measure of security that depends on defensive force, and within the measure of our resources we can give leadership in such a coalition. But only if we have a policy of our own. We can play an important part in appropriate collective arrangements. We can speak with a clear voice and we can take initiatives and promote ideas of far-reaching importance. We can generate enthusiasm and work diligently. All these things we can do with this independence which we claim as a free and sovereign nation. What we cannot do, however, is to pursue a policy inconsistent with the common goals.
If, as has been widely agreed, we depend for our survival as a free nation on mutual co-operation, then we must accept the reasonable conditions of that mutual co-operation. This does not imply subservience, but a true team spirit, comradeship and dedication to unity of purpose. Under these circumstances it is not possible to consider our defence posture in isolation, but only in the context of total western strength and policy.
There has been a great deal of talk about the possibility of disarmament. It is the goal which we must pursue with diligence and perseverance, but any agreement to disarm must contain satisfactory provisions for inspection and control. So far it has been impossible, Mr. Chairman, to achieve anything on this basis. We must pursue and search for agreement while at the same time maintaining our strength until disarmament has become a reality. In the meantime, the chances of success are far greater if the western world is negotiating from strength and not from weakness. Presently the balance of military power still remains with the west. I think the minister concurs in this view; he has stated so publicly on a number of occasions.
The capacity of the United States strategic air command is very great indeed. Last spring I had the pleasure, along with some other members of this House of Commons and of the other place, of visiting the headquarters of the strategic air command at Omaha, Nebraska. The briefing we received was very
Supply-National Defence thorough and very reassuring in regard to the efficiency of that organization. General Thomas S. Power, commander in chief of SAC, answered our questions frankly and fully, which I might say was a most refreshing change for some of us.
There is no doubt in my mind, that the strategic air command stands on guard for the western world and that without the deterrent which it in part provides soviet imperialism might not have been contained even to the extent that it has been contained during the past decade.
Not only does the strategic air command have an overwhelming retaliatory capacity, but unquestionably at this moment it would be able to get through the Russian defences and reach its targets. The organization and communications of this command are of an order of magnitude probably unprecedented in the military history of the world. As is well known a substantial percentage of its bombers are on a 15-minute alert at all hours of the day and night. In the case of an alert they are put into the air and headed in the direction of their targets in case an alert should develop under any circumstances into an all-out nuclear attack. At a certain predetermined point, however, as is well known, they automatically return to their bases unless given positive, incontrovertible instructions to proceed on the basis of an authorization from the President of the United States of America.
The strategic air command comprises the bulk of the western deterrent and retaliatory power. The remainder lies with the bombers of the Royal Air Force and with the atomic bomb carrying strike attack aircraft stationed in Europe under NATO command.
This western military superiority in the nuclear and thermonuclear field has been overwhelming until recently. Now the Russians are narrowing the gap. They appear to be concentrating their efforts in the missile field, and in this field they have achieved remarkable success.
There are three main components to an intercontinental ballistic missile; the propellant, the guidance mechanism and the nose cone. In two of these, the guidance mechanism and the nose cone, the achievements of Russia and of the United States are not too far apart. In the field of propellants, however, the Russians have a considerable advantage over their western competitors. Both sides have perfected this weapon to the point where it has intercontinental capability of amazing and frightening accuracy. This is all the more remarkable when we recall that it is only three years since the first sputnik was placed in orbit,
7562	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence and not long before that military scientists were saying that they would not live to see the day when the intercontinental ballistic missile would be operational. This incredible change in military science in the short space of three years has altered many of the traditional concepts and put great strain on our capacity to understand their implications.
Because of the intercontinental ballistic missile and its capability of knocking out retaliatory power on the ground, it has been widely suggested that the strategic air command should put its bombers on a continuous airborne alert. The United States government has taken the position that it is not yet necessary to do so. Their stand is based on the belief that the Russians do not yet have enough ballistic missiles to knock out the major portion of United States retaliatory strength on the ground, and that view would seem to be confirmed by what the minister said today.
In other words, even with a surprise attack involving the use of all of Russia's existing missiles the United States would still have sufficient retaliatory capacity to survive such an attack and to inflict unacceptable damage on the Soviet empire. A sufficiently large number of United States bases would remain intact from which this retaliatory power could be launched.
At the present rate of production of Russian missiles, however, the situation is changing from month to month, and under these circumstances one would expect the United States strategic air command to commence something more than a token airborne alert within the next year or so. This will become, provided there is no disarmament agreement reached in the meantime, absolutely essential in order to ensure that sufficient retaliatory capacity is at all times available to inflict unacceptable damage on the Russians. Only in this event will the threat of massive retaliation remain effective.
In the meantime the United States will no doubt continue to develop new and mobile retaliatory capacity in anticipation of the day when its bombers will wear out. This capacity will be provided through a number of projects. For example, the Polaris missile will be carried by atomic submarines. These will be deployed at sea and will be relatively invulnerable to enemy attack. Missiles and bomb-carrying aircraft will be available for launching by ocean-going ships whose whereabouts and position will not be known to a potential enemy and will not therefore be vulnerable to enemy attack in the same way as fixed land installations would be vulnerable.

The United States is developing a new intercontinental ballistic missile which they call the Minuteman which may be installed on mobile carriers such as trains, barges, et cetera. By moving these about they will not be sitting ducks for Russian missiles as they would be if based on permanent installations.
There are many projects underway designed to increase the mobile retaliatory potential of the United States, but these illustrations will suffice to demonstrate the effort being made. They must provide sufficient deterrent power to make it inadvisable for any aggressor to commence a war in the knowledge that retaliation would be sure and devastating.
In the existing circumstances this capacity must be maintained as long as the Russians have the power to strike. It is, according to many military scientists, the first priority of defence preparedness. As the minister has stated on many occasions, however, it is not a field on which Canada has chosen to embark.
It is perfectly obvious, however, that within a few years-assuming no universal disarmament agreement in the meantime-that each side will have sufficient capacity to devastate all major enemy targets with power to spare. This extra capacity is referred to in Pentagon jargon as an over-kill capacity. In layman's language it just means that there is more than one missile or bomber available for each target. When each side has this tremendous destructive potential which cannot be nullified by a surprise attack, it would be unthinkable for either side to take the offensive. No rational person would take the responsibility for an attack which would bring complete and utter destruction on his country.
There would be in effect a sterilization of the offensive potential on each side, an uneasy stalemate with neither side daring to fall appreciably behind the capacity of the other. At this point I should like to assert that I agree with the minister in one respect, that the development and research into anti-missiles and other weapons must continue for the very reason he stated earlier and which I just repeated, that one side cannot under any circumstances allow itself to fall appreciably behind the capacity of the other.
It is necessary then to consider what might happen under these circumstances. First of all there is the virtual certainty of an acceleration in the ideological and economic offensive. Second, there is the real possibility of skirmishes or limited engagements where potential aggressors would commence at least by using conventional arms only. Third, there is always the possibility of an irrational

attack, the act of a mad man or the consequences of an accident or miscalculation. The latter possibility, miscalculation or accident, may constitute the greatest danger that threatens us.
Even a cursory examination of news dispatches indicates the extent to which the western world has fallen behind on the ideological and economic fronts. We have shown a great lack of imagination in taking advantage of available opportunities. We have underestimated or failed to accept the magnitude of the task, our effort being analogous to the moving of a mountain of sand with a teaspoon. The west will have to accept the challenge and not only accept it but take the initiative all along the front. Failure to do so will result in defeat notwithstanding any expenditures for military equipment.
The best thing that military preparedness can do is to buy time albeit at a very high price. The economic and ideological aspects of the cold war are integral parts of the problem we face. They must receive full attention and corresponding action. As this is a defence debate, however, I will put my emphasis on the defence aspects and leave discussion of the economic and ideological aspects for another occasion.
General Maxwell Taylor in his book "The Uncertain Trumpet" has raised a question in respect to the policy of reliance on massive retaliation. I might underline that this is really part and parcel of the great defence argument which now faces us not only in this country but in other countries of the western world. I found his book disappointing and contradictory.
The one central point he raised, however, was clear. That was that at the time when both sides have a tremendous nuclear and thermonuclear capacity, what happens if one side decides to commence a limited action without the use of these weapons? In other words, reliance on the threat of massive retaliation ceases to be valid at a time when a bluff is just a bluff, when neither side would dare to stake the annihilation of its peoples and territories on the winning of a minor political objective. Under these conditions a limited action anywhere in the world involving the use by the aggressor of conventional weapons only would require either sufficient conventional forces to stop the attack or the use by the defenders of atomic weapons.
General Taylor cited the example of Korea where, as a matter of national and United Nations policy, action was limited to conventional weapons even against the advice of the commanding general. He suggested a similar condition not only could but might easily arise again. He questioned whether 79951 0-478
Supply-National Defence the United States and its allies have sufficient conventional strength to meet such a possibility and suggested that it would be prudent to consider sufficient augmentation to give military commanders the capacity to fulfil their objectives in accordance with the policy laid down by their political employers. He argued that more ground troops are required along with greater mobility and conventional fire power. The argument is basically realistic and one which cannot be ignored.
Another possibility which cannot be ignored is the possibility of irrational attack. It is difficult to comprehend the frightening implications of such a development. Certainly, by the mid-1960's-when both sides will possess a tremendous offensive capacity -there will be in the normal conventional sense no such thing as adequate protection or defence. If the deterrent fails, if general nuclear war breaks out, defence is futile, just as victory is impossible. That is not to say, as the military men will argue, that every attacking plane or missile shot down might conceivably save the destruction of a military target or a town. This argument really resolves itself into a mathematical problem. If each side has two missiles or bombers designated for each target it would be of little comfort to shoot down one of them. Of course, if both missiles or bombers destined for any particular target were shot down, the target or the town might be spared.
The cost of providing even a minimal and at best partial defence, however, is so staggering as to almost exceed the comprehension. The cost is so staggering because of the problems involved. The problem is not just shooting down bombers but also missiles launched from bombers, ICBM's and missiles launched from submarines. At the present time, of course, there is no known defence against ballistic missiles so that it is not just a matter of cost but also of technical possibility. Even should a major scientific breakthrough occur, however, which might offer the possibility of an anti-missile, the cost of providing installations on the scale necessary for even a token defence is so great as to be impractical. Consequently, one is driven to consider the alternative of spending on other projects.
I come now to a consideration of Canada's present position. It is necessary to discuss Canada's part in the over-all strategy and to study the integration of Canadian effort as a part of the whole, unless we disengage from the whole, and I do not recommend that.
Once it was known that the Russians had developed the thermonuclear bomb and had

Supply-National Defence the means of carrying it to the North American continent a scramble began to make such preparations as would give warning of any impending attack and permit the destruction of as large as possible a proportion of the attackers. The radar warning lines were built and interceptor squadrons established. Canada continues to operate nine air defence squadrons equipped with the now obsolete CF-100 interceptors; interceptors so slow they could not overtake the latest passenger aircraft.
To supplement the interceptor squadrons the United States undertook the development of a number of ground to air missiles designed for use against the manned bombers. All of these concepts had their inauguration before the intercontinental ballistic missile became operational. Included amongst them is the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile intended to complement manned interceptors as a second line or area defence.
Soon after the present government took office it signed the NORAD agreement which placed all of the air defence of the North American continent under a single unified command. This agreement, in a sense, did not materially affect the situation except perhaps as to minor improvements in communications and reaction time, in addition to the other aspect of control. Using this agreement as an excuse, our government has stubbornly insisted on proceeding with the installation of the Bomarc missile, notwithstanding our objection that it is a fixed installation which will be extremely vulnerable to enemy mis-silry by the time the whole system becomes operational. Its decision to proceed with the construction of fixed missile bases is contrary to the advice of the best military scientists of the day and should be reversed.
The Canadian navy continues to be occupied primarily in the anti-submarine role. The government is still building destroyer escorts of the same type they built three years ago, notwithstanding the development, in the meantime, of new and swift atomic powered submarines.

Europe continues to be 12 interceptor squadrons and one army brigade group. The interceptor squadrons which were first line in 1956 have become increasingly obsolescent since. Last summer the present government announced its decision to replace eight of those squadrons with a version of the United States Starfighter interceptor, presumably designed to carry out a strike attack role. This is a development of considerable significance in that for the first time Canada has commenced on a policy of acquiring equipment capable of participating in the role of nuclear retaliation. The particular aircraft chosen for this job has been widely criticized and therefore it will ever remain a mystery why the Canadian government chose a high altitude air superiority fighter for conversion to a low altitude strike reconnaissance role. We in the Liberal opposition have maintained it was the wrong aircraft for the job. Superior aircraft were available and could have been in use sooner had the government so decided.
The remaining four squadrons of interceptors, according to the minister, are to continue in use for two more years, but after that what? The minister has given us no indication at all, neither in the committee nor again today, whether they will be replaced or withdrawn.
Our brigade group in Europe is inadequately equipped. This was made perfectly clear in the evidence given to the committee. The minister has indicated some minor acquisitions of new equipment, but at the same time he tells us the brigade troop is now trained to operate under nuclear conditions but without being equipped with nuclear weapons. At page 449 of the evidence of the special committee on defence expenditures, in reply to a question, the minister said:
Yes, definitely. All troops of the Canadian army are trained so that they can operate on a nuclear battlefield, as well as being trained for the other tasks which might confront them; that is, the prevention of the outspread of a local war, where it is not anticipated that nuclear weapons would be used; and they are trained to be able to fight not only on a conventional battlefield, but also on a nuclear battlefield.
In either case that implies that the forces should be completely mobile; that they should be equipped with short range aircraft with helicopters, with amphibious carriers and so forth. We are advised, however, that none of this equipment is in the hands of the brigade group at the present time and that no money is included in the current estimates for procurement of these arms.

In reply to the minister, let me say that troops which are properly equipped and mobile would have the equipment to deal with any of those situations without a crisis arising and that is exactly our objection to the policies of this government. They make nothing but crises decisions.
What about Suez?
The government has left our brigade group ill equipped to do the job it might have to do, and the remedy is not in sight.
What about Suez?

I have the Suez situation in mind when I make some of the suggestions included in this statement, and the hon. member should listen because he might learn something. I repeat, the government has left our brigade group ill equipped to do the job it might have to do and the remedy is not in sight. Yet the brigade group is still expected to do its job. It is little short of criminal negligence to permit the situation to continue.
Another new situation is the question of atomic arms. This has become a very urgent factor. Confused and conflicting statements on the part of various members of the government have left the situation completely up in the air. Announcements have been made that three items of equipment will be purchased, about which the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 1223 of Hansard oi February 20, 1959:
The full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear weapons.
These include weapons for our NATO forces and for home defence. For NATO, our eight squadrons of new strike attack aircraft are to be equipped with atomic bombs. At the same time, as has been made perfectly clear from the evidence, no agreement has been reached with the French government in respect of stationing on French soil Canadian squadrons so equipped. Furthermore, according to the Minister of National Defence, no negotiations have yet taken place on the governmental level, although he states there have been preliminary discussions at the military level through the supreme allied commander in Europe. It seems difficult to believe that the government of Canada would go ahead and commit itself to the purchase of this equipment before arrangements were finalized for its use.
It is true that we do have two air bases in Germany and presumably F-104's could operate from them. In the day of missiles, however, it would seem sheer folly to station eight squadrons of atomic equipped planes on two

Supply-National Defence bases where they are vulnerable to sneak attack. We urge and demand that the government communicate to the house exactly what plans it has for the effective use of these machines.
The only other weapon on the government's present list which can utilize an atomic warhead is the Honest John ground to ground missile. This is a heavy and cumbersome piece of artillery but it is transportable by air if air transport is available.
With respect to North American defence, the government has committed itself to the use of the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile which even its staunchest supporters have never claimed to be effective without an atomic warhead. The government has committed the Canadian taxpayers to an expenditure of approximately $120 million for the SAGE-Bomarc system before it has made up its mind whether or not it will allow atomic warheads to be stored on Canadian soil. Without them the expenditure is useless but the decision has not yet been taken. It is a question of spending the money first and making the decision afterwards, a decision which might nullify the value of that expenditure.
The Prime Minister has said repeatedly that any atomic warheads stored in Canada would be under Canadian control. Obviously, however, this is not possible under United States law. The most that could be conceivably expected, would be so-called joint control. This is an arrangement under which Canada would have the discretion whether to use atomic warheads but only after they had been released to Canada by the President of the United States. It would be a question of whether to use uncle's car but only after uncle had decided it would be safe to turn over the key.
In summation, we allege that the present government has no defence policy. Its statements and actions with respect to air defence are confused and contradictory. It plans to re-equip our air division overseas with an aircraft which is virtually, I believe a re-design, notwithstanding government statements to the effect that we are no longer in the development business. It continues to build ships which may well be obsolete by the time they are launched. It organizes our brigade group for atomic war while at the same time denying it the necessary mobility and fire power. It involves us in the acquisition of weapons which only reach their full potential when armed with atomic warheads before any decision has been reached whether or not to so equip them. All in all, Mr. Chairman, the government's fumbling in defence matters is a sad and sorry mess. Our objection is not that they are spending too much
[Mr. Hellyer.l

or too little money but that what they do spend is not spent wisely or well. The objects of many of their expenditures are obsolete or pointless.
We asked for a special committee in order that a thorough study might take place. We asked the government to state a policy, a coherent, full and complete policy. Failing that, we felt we would be obliged, in keeping with our responsibility to the Canadian people, to indicate an alternative. The committee met but witnesses were not called. The minister failed to clear up the existing confusion. In opposition we do not have the advice of the chiefs of staff and we do not have access to classified data. Notwithstanding the limited information available to us, however, we feel obliged to live up to our undertaking and to indicate what we believe to be a sensible alternative to the government's confused lack of policy.
Based on all existing evidence, we believe that the Russians are not yet in a position to wage an all-out war with any hope of success. The minister re-emphasized that this afternoon and that is one point on which we agree. During the next two or three years the likelihood of a planned, calculated allout attack is not very great. In our suggestions, therefore, we have projected on this basis to the circumstances we expect several years hence at a time when the Soviet union will have a very large missile inventory which will neutralize and be neutralized by the striking capacity of the United States.
My first heading in this regard is continental air defence. By that time effective defence of the North American continent in the traditional sense will not be practical. Even if there should be a scientific breakthrough in the anti-missile field, it is not likely that the defence could overtake the tremendous lead presently enjoyed by the offence. Under these circumstances the main continuing function of what is presently continental air defence will be detection and identification. These are continuing requirements. Speaking to the NATO parliamentary group in Washington on November 18, 1959, General Kuter said:
We must first know what is present in our air space. Next, we must identify the object as friendly by one of several available methods. Failing in this, we classify the object as unknown, which necessitates an immediate scramble of an interceptor to visually examine the unknown.
As I stated earlier, it is likely that within the next year or so the strategic air command will find it necessary to commence a significant airborne alert. When it does, there will be hundreds of SAC bombers flying each way across Canada daily. These bombers will pass through our radar warning lines, the

D.E.W. line and the mid-Canada line. There is no problem in this as long as the communications systems remain intact but if they are disrupted problems arise. For example, if Russian trawlers were to cut trans-Atlantic telephone communications, as they have done, SAC bombers leaving European and African bases and coming to North America over the great northern route would have to rely on radio communications for the filing of flight plans. Radio communications though usually reliable are subject to wide fluctuations and at times are quite undependable. There is the possibility, therefore, of SAC bombers appearing on our radar screens as unidentified objects. Consequently, it is desirable that we have some equipment capable of undertaking a positive indentification. I might add that sometimes commercial aircraft fail to file flight plans. One case I remember well is when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport left for Winnipeg and wound up in Quebec city. This is just one other example of an occasion when it is better to send up an aircraft to take a look than to send up a Bomarc and say goodbye.
Do you believe that?

speechtext: You said goodbye to a lot of your friends who were once here.

Our present equipment allocated to this task of identification is the CF-100 interceptor. This plane is far too slow to overtake the fastest bombers in the Russian inventory. Obviously, therefore, if the identification role is to be carried out satisfactorily we must have a supersonic aircraft at least twice as fast as the one at present in service, one capable of a reserve of speed sufficient to allow early identification. The United States air force is very anxious that Canada should take such action, so anxious, indeed, that it has agreed to purchase from Canadair Limited of Montreal a number of CL-44 carriers if the Canadian government will at the same time buy a number of United States supersonic interceptors as replacements for the CF-100.
There has been considerable objection raised in the United States senate to the possibility of the United States air force buying Canadian planes. It was overcome, however, on the basis that the deal would be good for both countries. Because of the nature of the arrangement there would be no appreciable balance of payments problem and the employment created on one side of the border would approximately equal that enjoyed on the other side. The number of interceptors acquired would not be nearly as great as the number of CF-lOO's presently in our nine
Supply-National Defence squadrons. Perhaps the number which would be acquired under this arrangement would be sufficient for this role.
After consideration of all the factors involved we would recommend the acceptance of this proposal. I think the minister concurs with this suggestion, we hope he will, and that he will endorse it before the debate is concluded. The advantages to both countries are considerable. Canada would obtain a supersonic interceptor which would carry out the identification role and also, because it would be available immediately, it would provide some limited defensive capacity during the next two or three years. It would seem preferable that this role, which of necessity must be carried out over Canadian skies, should be done by the Royal Canadian Air Force and Canadian airmen. From the commercial standpoint, Canadair would obtain an advantage in cost which would put it in a more competitive position in regard to future sales of the same aircraft to commercial carriers. This would be a most welcome boost to Canada's failing aircraft industry.
Because of our belief that from the midsixties on there will be no possibility of effective air defence of the North American continent we can see no reason for continuing with the installation of equipment designed exclusively for that purpose. It is our contention, therefore, that the government should discontinue at once its participation in the SAGE-Bomarc system, and not proceed with the installation of radar gap fillers. These are only useful against attack by manned bombers. We contend that the possibility of attack during the next two or three years is not very great, and this is the only period during which these installations would be worth while. Interestingly enough, this would be the period during which they would be still under construction, not yet operational. By the time they are in place they will be obsolete, because by that time an all-out offence would involve the overwhelming use of missiles against which there is no defence.
Elimination of the SAGE-Bomarc system in Canada would eliminate the necessity for Canada storing or using atomic warheads on Canadian territory. The supersonic interceptors, which we would be acquiring under this arrangement, could be armed with conventional guided missiles such as the sidewinder. There would then be no immediate question of extending control of atomic weapons to another power. I know that this is a matter of great concern, not only to us on this side of the house but to the government, the Prime Minister and to others.
Then, in respect of NORAD, may I say that the leader of the Liberal party has stated from time to time that we believe NORAD

We are not satisfied, on the information given us, that this liaison requires Canadian membership in NORAD as an organization outside the NATO command structure. We think it is one which reflects the form more than the substance of partnership. On the basis, however, that our future contribution is confined to the detection and identification roles, we would not withdraw from NORAD unless it could be positively shown that the necessary liaison was possible outside of that organization.
I come now to NATO. At the time the NATO agreement was signed the objective was to build up in Europe a shield consisting of a substantial number of divisions armed with conventional weapons. Subsequently, however, at a time when the United States still had overwhelming superiority in atomic capability the NATO forces were reorganized along the lines dictated or at least rationalized by the theory of massive retaliation. More recently the European NATO shield has been described as a trip wire, a defensive force which would cause any attacker group to pause long enough that a rational decision must be taken before proceeding further with the attack, presumably in the knowledge that to proceed would bring about an all-out, unlimited war. This theory loses its validity, however, when the time comes that the threat of nuclear retaliation is merely a threat. When the offensive capability of each side is neutralized by the other the only way to stop a ground attack would be with those forces immediately available for that purpose. For this reason, we urge the NATO alliance to take cognizance of the future situation and to reorganize and rebuild its forces to the point required to stop a conventional attack by conventional means.
We believe that there should be a complete re-examination of the defence strategy of the NATO alliance to this end. Until that is completed and the Canadian role can be assessed in the light of its result the brigade group should remain in Europe in its present role. We deplore, in any event, its lack of more up to date equipment for its presently assigned task. We recommend that it be supplied with aircraft, helicopters and amphibious equipment necessary to give it the maximum flexibility. We would also recommend a policy of supplying it with up to date weapons with the maximum firepower.
Would the hon. member answer the question which he asked me to defer as to whether or not he would provide nuclear weapons?

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock we were discussing the alternative policy being put forward by this party in respect to the re-equipment and redirection, in a sense, of our armed forces. We had just completed discussion in respect to the brigade group in Europe.
With respect to the air division, we regret the decision of the government to re-equip on the basis of the strike attack role. Canada has not, in the past, contributed to the offensive potential in any way, and especially any nuclear potential. We feel that it is unnecessary and unwise to change this basic policy. Re-equipping the air division in this way creates a number of problems. Included in these is the possibility of duplication of targets between NATO's tactical bomb-carrying aircraft and the bombers and missiles of the strategic air command. It creates a serious problem as to the bases from which these planes can be operated and, above all, it creates the problem of the use by Canadian forces in Europe of nuclear weapons under national and not under collective control. By "national" I mean United States control.
If such weapons, even tactical defensive ones, are to be used as part of NATO defence forces, this should only be as a result of a collective NATO decision and if they are brought under NATO's collective control. Furthermore, we have no confidence in the aircraft chosen. We have never been able to understand why the government would choose a high altitude air superiority fighter converted to a low altitude striker role. Indeed, the long period of time which has elapsed between the selection of this plane and the present, when we are informed that the prototype has not yet been completed, is indicative of the extent to which modifications were necessary. This amounts practically to the development of a new aircraft, at a time when the Prime Minister has told us that Canada is no longer in the aircraft development business.

We also note that even after continued efforts the major accident rate of those models of this aircraft presently in use remains approximately double that of other "Century class" interceptors. Under these circumstances we would recommend cancellation of the acquisition of the CF-104 and the abandonment of Canada's offensive role.
Canada has no offensive role.

We suggest that the air division in Europe should be given a ground support role designed to give ground cover and tactical support to our brigade group. The aircraft chosen for this role, a new aircraft, would be one which could be utilized similarly in any trouble spot in the world where Canada's forces might be engaged.
Here again we would emphasize the international character of our defence policy and forces. This type of air support and air cover would be extremely valuable in circumstances of brush wars, limited engagements, et cetera, where perhaps United Nations action might be required, as well as in defence against conventional attack in Europe. The contribution it would make might be of significant importance, whereas in the event of an allout attack we cannot imagine that a few strike attack aircraft armed with small atomic bombs are going to alter significantly the outcome.
In respect to the Canadian navy, at the present time the Canadian navy is assigned almost exclusively to the role of anti-submarine warfare. Based on the belief that after the mid-19 60's real defence is impossible, the navy's anti-submarine role will be like any other form of defence, only partial and inadequate as far as the protection of the Canadian nation and all our peoples is concerned. Destroyer escorts presently being built are not as fast as contemporary submarines being built by the United States and Russia. They are also more vulnerable. Continuance of this program beyond the present strength seems to us quite unrealistic. In these circumstances the government should consider the possibility of replacing the six destroyer escorts in the current program with ships designed to act as combat troop carriers and supply ships, useful among other things for United Nations service. These could be used as bases for launching and supporting land operations in areas inaccessible to long range transport aircraft. These ships would increase the flexibility of Canada's mobile tactical forces and would add considerably to our capacity to react to United Nations requests involving international police action. Last night the minister spoke of mobility, transport mobility; but surely forces which
Supply-National Defence do not have sea support miss in one essential respect the all-round type of tactical transport and support which might, under some circumstances, be required.
The hon. member for Edmonton West stated this afternoon-at least, he reminded me to think back to the Suez situation. I am thinking back to when the Canadian aircraft carrier had to be stripped of its equipment in order to provide transport. It was not subsequently used, but the capacity was not at that time there which was considered essential and which might, under different circumstances, have been essential. Similarly, the minister told us in a statement-
Could I ask a question?

As soon as I am finished you can ask all the question you want. The minister also mentioned that troops should have the capacity of meeting commando operations anywhere in Canada, and yet very large portions of this country, including a great part of our sea coast, are inaccessible by air. They are inaccessible in any way except by sea, and certainly the type of mobility we have in mind here would add something to the general flexibility and capacity of tactical forces.
With respect to air transportability the Liberal party once again urges that the government's present program in respect to air transportability be augmented. It recommends an increase in the number of long range transport aircraft, sufficient to permit the simultaneous airlift of one brigade. This capacity would be available to transport Canadian troops to trouble spots anywhere in the world, which would tremendously increase Canadian capacity to respond to United Nations requests for immediate assistance. This capacity would be available, not only for transporting troops but for evacuating refugees, transporting food and supplies, et cetera. This capacity to airlift the brigade would be true air transportability. Again, the events of the last two weeks have demonstrated the necessity for this.
In the Congo situation you had practically an exclusive airlift by the United States military air transport service. It could easily happen that a situation will arise where for one reason or another it was not advisable to use military transport of the United States. Under those circumstances a large capacity for a Canadian airlift would prove extemely valuable and could be of great assistance not only to those troops or personnel we might be supplying in that particular situation but also to other nations with whom we might be co-operating.
Now as to research. This party believes that one of Canada's greatest contributions

Supply-National Defence to collective defence is in the field of defence research. We contend that we have the scientists and the capacity to undertake pure and applied research far in excess of the present level. We would recommend that expenditures in this field be augmented by annual increments until a level considerably higher than that of the present one is achieved. As a general policy we should undertake on behalf of the western world any research projects within our capacity referred to us. At the same time we would be able to put forward our own ideas and the method of selection would not be too different from that presently employed by the defence research board. We believe that many of these projects could be carried out at Canadian universities and by Canadian industry on behalf of the defence research board.
In the field of applied research we recommend the development of some equipment in fields where it is believed that Canada could become pre-eminent. We realize that there are a few limited projects which might come within this class or category at the present time, but very few. These areas of development would provide the technical and industrial know-how which would permit Canada to compete in world markets in respect of the commercial equivalents and derivatives of such development. This specialization would provide steady growth for the export of Canadian manufactured goods.
There is one major area of development which we feel would be a challenge to Canadian capacity, and particularly suited to Canadian needs. It is the development of atomic engines for use in transportation, particularly as applied to aircraft. This is a project with virtually unlimited civil and defence applications.
We are told that the Russians are developing atomic powered aircraft and that the west is falling behind in this race. It is also forecast that atomic powered aircraft will, to an extent at least, supersede the guided missile. It would be capable of flying for virtually unlimited periods at low altitudes at supersonic speed and will render existing radar equipment and allied paraphernalia obsolete. As a component of a deterrent force it will be mobile and virtually invulnerable, being at the same time capable of carrying and launching ballistic missiles with deadly accuracy. Commercial and other applications are virtually unlimited and test the imagination to conceive. This would not only be an unique and urgent contribution to the collective defence of the west but would also be of vital importance to Canada's industrial potential.
[Mr. Hellyer.I

Unquestionably the day will come when there will be a very large world-wide market for small and medium sized atomic reactors and engines. Canada as one of the world's leading uranium producers will be vitally interested in supplying fuel for this market. The market, however, will likely be available to those who are best equipped through experience and capacity to provide the complete package. For this reason future uranium sales would hinge to a large extent on Canada's ability to capture for itself a sizeable proportion of the world reactor market. Seldom has a country been faced with such a promising challenge of such great opportunity. This is not the first time I have put forward this suggestion. It is in fact a restatement of a proposal I made at the national Liberal convention in January, 1958. I believe, however, it is one worthy of implementation without further delay.
It has been stated that Canada cannot afford to undertake any major developmental projects. This view has been widely accepted and is held by the present government. Obviously, however, if there are 15 major developmental programs required to be done by the western world Canada should be able to afford and should undertake one of them. The United States with her great resources can well afford to do many, but at least we should do our proportionate share. The attitude of the present government reminds me of the parable of the talents. Discovering to its horror that Canada had only one talent, our government decided to bury it in the ground. This is a negative and passive approach to the use of our resources. There is, of course, always the risk of failure and failure is embarrassing. A government with courage, however, would not turn its back on the course it believed to be right, simply because of the element of risk involved.
All of these suggestions have been based, of course, on the premises stated. These, unfortunately, include no general disarmament agreement. This party has urgently stressed the importance of trying to arrive at an agreement which would reduce the likelihood of the possibility of an atomic war or indeed of any war. We still believe that all efforts should be bent in this direction. Any agreement, to be workable, however, must have effective provisions for inspection and control. Today's discussion is based on the conditions existing in the world today, that no such agreement has yet been reached and that the possibility of living through a long period under what might be called the era of thermonuclear terror is a

real possibility. If this is so, civil defence becomes a much more urgent problem.
In an extended period where each side in the cold war possesses the power of thermonuclear destruction there exist two possibilities of catastrophe. First, if one side thought it had an overwhelming military superiority which would enable it to launch a surprise attack and survive retaliation there could be the temptation of a calculated risk. Much more likely, however, would be the possibility of a war started by a madman or as the result of an accident or incident. Should this occur there is no real protection against disastrous destruction. There is the possibility, however, of saving a good proportion of our population by taking adequate steps to protect against radiation.
It is obvious from talking to Canadians in all walks of life and reading letters to editors that we have, as a people, been brainwashed. We have adopted the fatalistic attitude that in the event of an all-out war all is lost and there would be no survival. It would be the end of civilization, it is said, like "On the Beach". This fatalistic viewpoint is just not sound. "On the Beach", written by the late Nevil Shute, is science fiction and does not purport to be technically accurate. In the event of all-out war millions of people would be saved if fall-out shelters were available. From the standpoint of survival alone this is just about the most effective way in which we can spend money on defence against attack. Over a period of years, for a small proportion of our national budget we could provide survival for a large proportion of our people.
Furthermore, it has been asked "What is the sense of surviving if one takes into account the conditions of radiation which would exist in the post-attack environment?"
This case is very well stated by Rogers Cannell, manager of the industry and civil defence research, Stanford research institute in an article entitled "Civilization Can Recover" in which he states:
Many accept the idea that shelter can effectively reduce casualties but believe that survival in the post attack environment would be impossible. They fear the invisible and mysterious atomic radiation and believe that recovery from the loss of a major portion of the nation would be impossible.
A radioactive environment will take its toll. This fact must not be minimized. But it is also important to know that its toll is not worse than a setback of only a few decades in medical history. Our lives would be as long as our grandfathers' and the proportion of stillborn children and child deformities should be no worse than 30 years ago. In fact, the post-attack environment with our present state of medical knowledge would be somewhat safer than the one most of us entered at birth.

The author goes on to draw examples from history including one from the thirty years* war. One or two of my newspaper friends have told me I should not refer to such an historical example so I will not. But if I were to mention it I would merely say-
Go ahead.

-that history does offer additional evidence that a civilization can recover from a devastating war. In the words of Mr. Cannell:
Take, for example, the thirty years' war-an ideological conflict fought in central Europe in the first half of the 17th century. The loss of life due directly to the war has been placed by the lowest estimate at one third of the entire population of both Germany and Bohemia. Other estimates run as high as 80 per cent. The social effects were catastrophic-entire districts were turned into deserts, wolves ran in the streets of once populated cities, and cannibalism was widespread. Yet, in a generation or so these areas had recovered in most respects. After a nuclear attack, short in duration, and starting from a much higher base of knowledge, recovery would be far easier for us. War must be prevented at any cost-
I wish to underline this. The goal of all our policies and proposals on both sides of the house is equally dedicated to one important realization and that is the avoidance of war. If there is any difference between us it is merely on the means of achieving this end. Again in the words of the author:
War must be prevented at any cost-and protection and preparation for recovery are part of that cost. But war is not the end of civilization. We must take every step we can now to accelerate the recovery process.
Believing this proposal to be fundamentally sound we urge steps to accelerate rapidly a national capacity to survive a nuclear holocaust. Like any other insurance it will be expensive, but it is certainly far more urgent and necessary than many of the ways we presently spend our national income.
Before leaving the subject of civil defence I want to admit that I am a recent convert to this way of thinking. Until recently, at least, like many other people I wondered just what efforts could be taken that would be of any use, if indeed there were steps which could be taken, which would justify the expense and which would offer some reasonable insurance in case of all-out attack. After giving the matter considerable study, however, I have come to the conclusion that under these circumstances-under the circumstance of an uneasy period of years when both sides have the capacity of total thermonuclear annihilation-we have no alternative but to try and take such steps as we can to protect the largest possible proportion of our civilian population.

Supply-National Defence
I believe this to be urgent. I think the minister, to at least a certain extent, agrees with this. I hope that we will have a more realistic attitude toward this matter of civil survival which up until now has been more a matter of games, planning and the passing of papers than it has a real and vital program.
In summation then, the Liberal policy is designed to meet in the best way possible the following conditions:
1.	To spend those funds set aside for national defence effectively and wisely.
2.	To contribute to our collective alliances those components which continue to be useful.
3.	To build forces flexible enough to respond to virtually any United Nations request for assistance; forces in being, fully equipped, fully mobile and transportable by air or sea; forces capable of effectively participating in any brush fire or conventional encounter before it gets out of hand with the possibility of triggering a wider conflagration.
4.	To build forces which would be useful as part of a world police force in the event a disarmament agreement should be reached.
5.	To contribute to research to the end that the western world forge ahead in scientific development keeping in mind also the economic by-products which might accrue.
6.	To provide the maximum protection possible to the Canadian population in the event of irrational attack.
7.	To promote an even more effective Canadian contribution to the preservation of world peace.
Mr. Chairman, we believe that the suggestions we have made will contribute materially to these objectives. Before resuming my seat I should like to deal briefly with one or two of the comments made by the minister at the conclusion of his remarks. Unfortunately, I have not had an opportunity to examine his address in detail so I will deal with the other points later.
The minister tried to leave the impression that by a policy of not having Bomarcs and nuclear warheads for Bomarc the Canadian nation was being placed in jeopardy. Nothing could be further from the truth. If we believed for one moment that the Bomarcs provided any real protection with or without nuclear warheads we would concur in their use, but we do not believe so. On the contrary, we think they are nothing but an added liability. We think they would put in jeopardy the survival of people in the immediate area because they would in fact become one of the few priority targets in this country.
In our minds it is not a question of using a missile with an atomic warhead such as the Bomarc. It is our conclusion after serious consideration that in the time period in which


these missiles will be in operation they will provide no effective defence whatsoever and might just as well not be there. If anyone else thinks differently let him support the policy and let him pay the piper. We do not believe so. We particularly do not believe so when the atomic warheads would be under the control of the United States government.
That is not correct. The hon. member knows that is not correct.

With respect to atomic weapons being used by NATO, as we have stated we urge a complete revaluation of the NATO policy to determine if it would not be possible to build up conventional forces. We have stated that we would not wish to anticipate the results of such reconsideration. If after this reconsideration it was felt that situations might arise when nuclear defensive weapons have to be used, then we would urge, provided it was a collective agreement, that these weapons be supplied and used or not used in respect to a collective NATO agreement.
There is nothing unreasonable about this. Our position has been logical and straightforward. We do not believe, however, that it is necessary for Canada to embark on a new role in Europe which it has never had, a role of strike attack with Canadian aircraft, carrying atomic bombs, which can penetrate enemy territory and be part of the retaliatory forces if so decided.
Coming and going at the same time.

I am sure that on reflection the minister will see the error of the early and hasty remarks he made, and we would be pleased to hear from him further in this regard as the debate continues. We will take another look at his statement, because our purpose is to try as best we can to contribute to a pool of ideas and the working out of solutions which are in the best interests of this country. I do not think any hon. member would deny this motive to anyone on any side of the house. We are not for one moment detracting from the sincerity of the government in what it is doing. All we are saying is that we disagree with the mechanics and with some of the specific proposals which the government has placed before this house.
In conclusion, in respect of the incident that happened today, I should just like to say that I had a few typewritten copies of my speech which I gave to a number of newspaper reporters who asked for them until all of the copies were gone. Each copy was marked "For release on delivery". I cannot believe that a newspaperman, or a newspaper, would deliberately violate the agreement under which advance copies of speeches are

made available to them. I am sure that from time to time accidents do happen. This is not the first time that speeches have been printed by mistake in advance of delivery. I do not believe it was done wilfully, but-

I doubt whether there will be any question that we need common sense instead of nonsense in national defence. In trying to present what I think is a policy of common sense in national defence I am arranging what I have to say so as to make a number of references to NORAD, to Bomarc and to NATO. Then, I hope to enlarge upon these three matters from the C.C.F. point of view and to conclude my remarks with a definite statement of 11 points of C.C.F. policy as far as national defence is concerned.
The C.C.F. insists that there is no defence against thermonuclear weapons; therefore we maintain that NORAD is useless and that Canada should immediately withdraw from this alliance. The Bomarc, even if it were armed with a nuclear warhead, could never possibly shoot down enough bombers to prevent annihilation in a single attack. We feel that it is madness to think that any aggressor, if it were to attack North America, would do less than send all its available bombers in the first attack. If this is correct, and we think it is, then the Bomarc, just like the Arrow is a total waste of money from beginning to end.
The C.C.F. considers that NATO's heavy reliance on nuclear weapons is suicidal for this reliance leaves NATO only two choices for dealing with any aggressive soviet move in the NATO area, and that is either death or defeat. It means death in a thermonuclear holocaust, and that would be bound to result from the slightest use of nuclear weapons in Europe. Or it could mean defeat in a conventional war, because it is our understanding it is only the soviets who are fully equipped for conventional war. The C.C.F., therefore, insists that Canada must urge upon NATO a fundamental replacement of the present nuclear strategy; the C.C.F. also insists that Canada must urge that NATO honestly strive to work toward disengagement and disarmament in Europe.
We strongly feel that we must work toward the creation of a buffer zone in Europe at the same time as we make a buffer zone of Canada. When we use the term "buffer" we do so in the sense of the dictionary definition. The concise Oxford dictionary defines "buffer" as a neutral state lying between two larger ones serving to render less possible hostilities between them. Of course, in speaking of Canada as a small state, I am speaking in the military sense as compared with the major powers.
I think I am safe in saying that the basic trouble with our Canadian national defence policy is that those who are responsible for it
7574	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence cannot or will not understand one fundamental fact, namely that there is no defence against thermonuclear weapons and a war fought with such weapons would be suicidal. It therefore follows, in my opinion at least, that all defensive preparations for such a war are a waste of time, energy and money. Worse yet, such defensive preparations increase the ghastly possibilities of thermonuclear war by letting people think that defence is possible against thermonuclear war and that therefore a policy which could lead to thermonuclear war is not automatically idiotic. A national defence policy which includes the possibility of national suicide is a contradiction in terms.
It should be clear-we hope it is clear- that thermonuclear war would be national suicide since no amount of air defences, no amount of counterattacks, will prevent sufficient thermonuclear weapons getting through to destroy the nation. Therefore I insist and the C.C.F. insists that logic insists that the basic aim of our national defence policy must be to prevent war. This means that we must lend every support to any reasonable plan for total world disarmament. Neither the U.S.S.R. nor the United States will divest themselves of their nuclear weapons until all other means of making war have disappeared.
I should like at this time to divert from the basic principles I have been trying to outline in order to speak on certain aspects and I will return to the basic principles in a few minutes. I should like to spend a little time on what I might term the German question and Berlin. Some 15 years after the end of the second world war Germany is divided and no peace treaty has been signed. Very strong conventional Russian forces surround the city of Berlin, fully strong enough to blockade the city and prevent us doing anything about it unless we are prepared to engage in a thermonuclear war. Defeat or death appear to be the only two alternatives in Berlin if the Russians start something, so we say surely it is not impossible to work out an agreement that will reconcile the minimum aims of both sides.
I admit, of course, that we will have to make concessions but so too will the Russians. After all, they would like to see all of Berlin fully integrated into communist East Germany and, of course, we will not let them have this and I think the Russians realize that they are not going to be allowed to have it. So I believe that we have got to try to get some sense into both sides. I admit that in saying that I am perhaps in the field of foreign policy but I do so because I think that we have to remember constantly the inter-relationship between foreign and defence policies.


When we think of Berlin and the entire problem of Germany we have to consider Europe and when we consider Europe we have to consider NATO. I say that regardless of why massive soviet forces are in eastern Europe, as long as they are there then NATO must be powerfully supported by the western allies. However, I do feel that the present military situation in Europe is that the NATO forces are greatly outnumbered by the Russians in effective combat formations. The western policy appears to be to balance NATO's weakness in conventional forces by being ready to use so-called tactical nuclear weapons. This appears to be a carry-over from the early days of NATO when it had nuclear superiority. But the west has absolutely no grounds for assuming that NATO still has this superiority, and it has still less reason for thinking that a weak force armed with nuclear weapons is going to beat a large force armed with nuclear weapons. What is important is to be able to counter any soviet move, such as a blockade of Berlin, with conventional forces.
The idea of meeting any and all soviet aggressions in the NATO area with nuclear weapons is, I think, highly dangerous. The interests of both sides, the interests of all are too vitally involved in Europe for a nuclear war there to remain a limited nuclear war. That is why we feel that Canada must insist that NATO recast its strategy, its tactics and its organization so that its defensive forces are capable of meeting any soviet aggression with conventional weapons long enough to allow diplomacy to seek a settlement before, progressively, tactical nuclear weapons and thermonuclear weapons are brought into use.
So long as NATO both earnestly endeavours to reach an agreement with the Warsaw pact countries on disarmament and disengagement and also simultaneously begins revising its present suicidal nuclear strategy, then we in the C.C.F. say that Canada should remain in and support the NATO organization.
I would be failing my responsibility if 1 expressed a view on defence and weapons in Europe and then did not come right back home, so I should like to have a few words to say on the question of NORAD. Within our own borders there is much that we can do to lessen the suicidal possibility of thermonuclear war. With the continual refinement of the methods of delivery of thermonuclear weapons, the terrible danger of a pre-emptive attack by one massive power on the other becomes more and more prevalent. Indeed with each of the two major powers thinking in terms of a pre-emptive attack on the other such an attack almost becomes a certainty.

Surprise is essential for a successful preemptive attack else the annihilation will be mutual. Anything that Canada can do, therefore, to reduce the fear of either side of a surprise attack would be a step toward the prevention of war. That is why I fully associate myself with my colleague, the hon. members for Kootenay West, who called in this house about three weeks ago for the internationalization of the D.E.W. line, thereby making of Canada a true buffer between the U.S.S.R. and the United States. However, I thought it would be understood that the suggestion of the internationalization of Canada's radar warning lines would be a policy proposal for all radar warning lines throughout the world to be internationalized.
Since thermonuclear war between the United States and the U.S.S.R. could only be national suicide for Canada as well as for the United States, it follows that only deterrence makes sense. Actual defence against thermonuclear weapons is useless. As I see it, there is no point in shooting down 500 bombers if 500 others get through and thereby destroy us. The North American air defence command, NORAD, is therefore useless and I think we should withdraw from the alliance. The strategic air command needs time to get its squadrons airborne and the D.E.W. line furnishes this time, not the interceptors or anti-aircraft missiles of NORAD. The whole idea of protecting SAC bases, of shooting down Soviet bombers, stems from the notion of actually fighting a thermonuclear war which, according to my understanding, is not possible by any nation in the world unless it wants to commit suicide.
I feel strongly that the CF-105, the Arrow, was a waste of money from beginning to end and that the Bomarc is no better. I say that regardless of whether the Bomarc has a high explosive or nuclear warhead because if a war starts then it is almost bound to be a thermonuclear war leading to destruction. It could start if any nation or government is crazy enough to trigger a third world war in our generation. I think that the Liberals are right in what they have said today in opposing the Bomarc. However, we think they are entirely wrong to go on from there and advocate the replacement of the CF-100 with a supersonic plane. Either we can develop an adequate defence for Canada against thermonuclear attack or we cannot. If we cannot, and it is the firm belief of the C.C.F. that we, and every other nation, cannot, then it is useless to go on spending hundreds of millions of dollars on Canadian air defence.

I listened very carefully to it, not only listened to it but I read it before you said it.
To have supersonic interceptors capable of identifying supersonic bombers would be nice, but would it be worth the hundreds of millions of dollars we would have to spend? I have my doubts that supersonic interceptors would deter supersonic bombers. If an aggressor were to decide on an all-out attack on this continent, and I cannot conceive of any aggressor making anything less than an all-out attack, enough bombers would undoubtedly get through even if we had the new and improved replacements.
Mutual deterrence alone unhappily, and I say unhappily, is still the only answer to a thermonuclear threat and in this Canada has no direct part. So we say, let us not continue fooling ourselves by talking continental air defence. It is time we cut our losses. It is time we got out of NORAD. It is time we devoted the money at present being wasted to trying to prevent war rather than continuing to prepare for suicide.
Then, of course, I come to the subject of the expenditure of money and that brings me to a reference to submarines. I have no hesitation in saying that I oppose the suggestion of the defence committee that Canada consider obtaining submarines. Submarines are weapons of all-out war and all preparations for actually fighting such a war just do not make sense in this day and age. If an all-out war were to break out how would one or 10 or 100 Canadian submarines save the nation? To do so, we would have to destroy every nuclear missile-firing submarine. We would have to do it within hours of war breaking out. I will admit that I cannot understand why there does appear to be so much deliberate propaganda from the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A. building up to an eventual war. I do not think either country wants war. However, we have to consider it from that basis. Now then if we do consider it from that basis we come right back to the question I mentioned, submarines. If there has to be this continual propaganda fight, then if my understanding is correct that the war will be an all-out war, a thermonuclear war, how can Canada with a few submarines prevent an all-out attack or an all-out war on a thermonuclear basis?
I think we have to face the facts, harsh as they may be and I admit they are harsh. We have to stop this defence policy of wishful thinking and, therefore, I maintain, the useless expenditure of money. I cannot repeat too often that what we have to do is prepare for peace. We do not do that by entering into a policy of buying submarines. They neither defend nor do they deter.

I was rather surprised by the statement made by the Minister of National Defence yesterday, which can be found on page 7522 of Hansard. The minister is reported as having said:
-the primary aim of our defence policy must be to prevent war, not to win a war but to prevent war, and thus the importance placed by the west on their deterrent power. In the past it has sometimes been politically desirable to avoid a war. Today nuclear weapons have created a situation in which the main if not the sole purpose of the armed forces is deterrence. To use our armed forces in action would mean, therefore, that the purpose for which we have kept them has failed.
Then, only a page later the minister said this:
If the armed forces are not ready when war breaks out there will be no opportunity to recover.
Then just a few lines farther on he is reported as saying:
These are, as I think the committee knows, first of all the provision of naval, air and ground forces for the defence of the Canada-United States region, in other words the North American continent;
If you put those remarks together, or if you try to, I think they conclusively prove that he does not understand what defence is all about in a thermonuclear age. I feel that he does not understand the fundamental difference between the defence of North America and defence of the NATO area. They are two entirely different things. The NATO area is contiguous to the soviet zone, and the whole range of military power is required in the NATO area, from an infantry platoon up to thermonuclear weapons, so that any soviet aggressive move may be deterred by the certainty of the appropriate NATO response. Therein, of course, lies the present danger in the NATO area, because NATO's weakness in conventional weapons forces it into two exclusive a reliance, I feel, on thermonuclear weapons. If they are ever used then I say, as the minister said, our defence policy has failed.
In North America I think the situation is different from that in NATO. It is ridiculous to think of any attack on North America as anything less than an all-out attack, and an all-out attack would automatically trigger the United States deterrent, that is the strategic air command. Therefore, in North America we do not need infantry platoons to balance or to deter anything from the U.S.S.R. What we need is what we have, that is the strategic air command and the means to alert the strategic air command, which we have, the D.E.W. line.
I feel the minister has been confusing defence and deterrence. Deterrence is a part of our defence policy, that is true, but defensive weapons are no deterrence against the only


weapons which could ever conceivably be used in an attack on the North American continent, namely thermonuclear weapons. There is no defence, we have been told time after time, against such weapons. Therefore, I feel it is the failure to understand this point that leads the present government, and led the Liberals, to spend millions of dollars on Bomarcs, interceptors and anti-submarine weapons. There is no defence against H-bombers, ICBM's and nuclear missile-firing submarines. I feel that when the minister referred, as he did, to the provision of naval, air and ground forces for the defence of the Canada-United States region, he showed that he does not understand that the defence policy for the North American continent can only rest on one thing, and one thing alone, that is deterrence, until disarmament can be achieved.
I notice, Mr. Chairman, that my time is running short. At first sight it may appear strange to advocate that Canada be a buffer zone at home and yet support NATO abroad. The reason stems from what must be the basic aim of our defence policy: to prevent war.
I want to state and make it very clear that neither neutrality nor pacifism is necessarily commendable in itself. The fact of the matter simply is that by being a buffer in North America Canada can best prevent an all-out pre-emptive war between the United States and the Soviet union. On the other hand, were we simply to quit NATO without making the slightest attempt to modify NATO's strategy and organization, we would not have done all we could to prevent world-wide war breaking out there, a war in which we would surely suffer annihilation. But I want to make entirely clear that there can be no question, as far as the C.C.F. is concerned, of Canada retiring into isolationism. Rather we say we must move forward from outdated military alliances into the broadest internationalism.
We say we must quit wasting money on air defence, that is, defence against H-bombers, ICBM's and nuclear missile-firing submarines, for all such defence is obsolete. We say we must devote our energies instead to preventing war by really doing our best to bring about a complete and universal disarmament, and by working hard to reduce the underlying tensions in the world which are the cause of war.
In summary, Mr. Chairman, I would like to offer these main points as the basis for a new and sensible defence policy for Canada, a defence policy which fully takes account of the fact that thermonuclear war would be

suicidal and that the task of our armed forces is to prevent war and not to prepare for suicide:
1.	Canada should immediately end the NORAD agreement.
